newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Unocal defends investment in oil field in Burma.
newsitem.headline: Unocal defends investment in oil field in Burma.

text.p: The Unocal Corp of the United States on Monday defended the company's investment in military-ruled Burma, highlighting the company's U.S. $6-million community project.

"From our point of view the best way to help Burma is to provide growth, provide opportunities, provide a growing economy, help in the development of the middle class, help in the development of all this infrastructure that needs to occur," William Ichord told Reuters in an interview.
Unocal is a stakeholder in Burma's Yadana offshore gas field which is expected to start producing 525 million cubic feet of gas per day in 1998 to feed a power plant in Thailand.
Plans for the field also include feeding gas to a power plant and fertilizer plant near Rangoon.

Oil companies, among the largest investors in Burma, have come under increasing pressure from human rights activists to withdraw from ventures with the military government, which has suppressed moves for greater democracy.
Several American businessmen, in Singapore for a one-day meeting of the U.S./ASEAN Business Council, said they preferred a policy of "constructive engagement" to move Rangoon towards democracy.

ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam follows such a policy of involvement, not isolation, to push for change.
Ichord, vice president of Unocal's Washington office, said Unocal agreed. Withdrawing from a project would not stop it. Another company would step in, he said.
"These projects will go forward. This is a known natural gas field or six trillion cubic feet. It's a valuable asset," Ichord said. Investment in the field is around $1.2 billion.
The investment also includes pumping $6 million into the Burmese community along the 39-mile (62 km) route of a pipeline that will take the gas across Burma and into Thailand.
"Virtually every project we go into...there is always some sort of community outreach type of project" including in the United States, Ichord said.
He said so far, human rights activists appeared to have ignored the community project, which is promoted by all the partners in the Yadan field.
"I am not sure they have focused on them. I think it is unfortunate they do not see that these are an important ingredient in helping the country," he said.
The land section of pipeline passes 13 villages with a combined population of around 35,000 people. About 2,000 Burmese are employed on the pipeline project.

The community project includes building, modernising and supplying hospitals and medical centres, supporting pig, poultry, goat and shrimp farming and an inoculation programme against a number of diseases.
Ichord said politics was a question for the Burmese.

"They have to resolve for themselves first and foremost their own political determination. When that is done, when Burma has made its decision on that, they need to have the type of infrastructure in place that we are developing," he said.

Unocal holds a 28.26 percent stake in the field. France's Total SA holds 31.24 percent, Petroleum Authority of Thailand Exploration and Production 25.5 percent and Burma's state-owned Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise 15 percent.
